name: Wood beam span
seoDesc: Wood beam span: work out beam span from the uniformly distributed load and the deflection due to loading. A free construction calculator with the formula,…
summary: Supply the uniformly distributed load, the deflection due to loading and the maximum allowable deflection and the Wood beam span calculator solves for beam span. That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Wood beam span calculator work?
sections.html:
The Wood beam span calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports beam span in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the wood species, the lumber grade and the beam size); then you type in the uniformly distributed load (w), the deflection due to loading (δ), the maximum allowable deflection (δₘₐₓ) and the bending stress (Fb).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Wood beam span calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Ek=(-(Height or depth (d) ^ 3) × deflection due to loading (δ) × Width or breadth (b) × (A × A + B × B + C × C + D × D + F × F + G × G + H × H) + (5 ÷ 32) × uniformly distributed load (w) × (beam span (L) ^ 4)) ÷ (ek × (Height or depth (d) ^ 3) × deflection due to loading (δ) × Width or breadth (b))
Beam span (L)=deflection limit criteria × maximum allowable deflection (δₘₐₓ)
A=(bending stress (Fb) − fb b × B − fb c × C − fb d × D − fb e × ek − fb f × F − fb g × G − fb h × H) ÷ fb a
A=(shear stress (Fv) − fv b × B − fv c × C − fv d × D − fv e × ek − fv f × F − fv g × G − fv h × H) ÷ fv a
Emin c=(-emin a × A − emin b × B − emin d × D − emin e × ek − emin f × F − emin g × G − emin h × H + minimum modulus of elasticity (Eₘiₙ)) ÷ C
Wet service factor (CM) for Fb=(((bending stress (Fb) × size factor (CF) > 1150) ? ( 17 ÷ 20 ) : ( 1 )))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in centimeters

  • Force per length, opening in newtons per meter
  • Length, opening in centimeters

  • Pressure, opening in megapascals

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Wood beam span calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the uniformly distributed load, the deflection due to loading and the maximum allowable deflection — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Wood beam span calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns beam span, derived from the uniformly distributed load, the deflection due to loading and the maximum allowable deflection. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Wood beam span calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the uniformly distributed load, the deflection due to loading and the maximum allowable deflection, which is 24 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter Width or breadth (b) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Width or breadth (b) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (9 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Width or breadth (b) = 0 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Wood beam span calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
